extraction_notes.note: The introduction's informal restatements of Theorem 5.2, Propositions 5.13, 5.16, 6.2, 6.6, 6.8, 6.9 and Corollary 5.19 get no nodes (the numbered environments are kept). The outlook paragraphs and the closing discussion of Section 6.1 (Severi-Brauer and Weil-restriction generalizations) are not extracted either.

The classification into Types 0-5 is a cited description list followed by two TikZ tables of curve configurations and toric polygons. The list is one external theorem node; the pictures are not extracted.

Definition or claim: each sentence introduces notation (the derived dual, the relative duality functor, the modules E_i) and also asserts a property (anti-autoequivalence, generation). Typed as definitions because the symbols are used later.

These numbered equations define objects (the bundles frak E_Z, h_d, M_d(X), F_d(X), the functors Phi_d). Kept as equation nodes as the numbered-equation rule requires, with definition-like uses edges from them.

Serre duality for Gorenstein schemes and the Picard lattice lemma are folklore (uncited), and Lemma 2.4 is attributed to Bridgeland. All three are marked external, while their proofs in the paper are origin paper.

Corollary 5.5 is justified only by the clause 'Considering base changes to geometric points of S and using Theorem 4.5, we obtain', which runs straight into the environment with no colon or period. That clause is used as a prose proof node.

The parser marks only the third item of the first itemize in the proof of Lemma 6.1 as an author label. Steps therefore start at that item, which splits the 'either ... or ... or' sentence across two steps.

Two finishing-step warnings are left in place because the symbol is used in another sense. E_i stands for both the exceptional divisors (Section 2) and the standard exceptional modules (Appendix A, used in the proof of Proposition 3.17). S_0 stands for both the open set S minus S_1 (Section 6.3) and the simple module (Appendix A).
The source says 'in case (3)' for the Jordan type labelled (2), and Lemma 5.9 has the typo 'compativle'. Both are copied verbatim.

nodes.statement: We show that the total space X of a flat family X to S of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with du Val singularities is regular if and only if the three schemes S, Z_2, and~Z_3, associated with it, are all regular (Proposition~); in the same vein, the morphism X to S is smooth if and only if the morphisms Z_2 to S and Z_3 to S are (Remark~).
conclusions: We show that the total space X of a flat family X to S of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with du Val singularities is regular if and only if the three schemes S, Z_2, and~Z_3, associated with it, are all regular (Proposition~); in the same vein, the morphism X to S is smooth if and only if the morphisms Z_2 to S and Z_3 to S are (Remark~).
nodes.raw_latex:
We show that the total space ${\mathscr{X}}$ of a flat family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with du Val singularities is regular 
if and only if the three schemes $S$, ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$, associated with it, are all regular (Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness});
in the same vein, the morphism ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ is smooth 
if and only if the morphisms ${\mathscr{Z}}_2 \to S$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3 \to S$ are (Remark~\ref{remark:smoothness}).
nodes.clean_text: We show that the total space X of a flat family X to S of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with du Val singularities is regular if and only if the three schemes S, Z_2, and~Z_3, associated with it, are all regular (Proposition~); in the same vein, the morphism X to S is smooth if and only if the morphisms Z_2 to S and Z_3 to S are (Remark~).

nodes.statement: For d le 4, however, the results of show that an S-linear semiorthogonal decomposition for a general flat family~X to S whose components are twisted derived categories of finite coverings of~S does not exist.
nodes.raw_latex:
For $d \le 4$, however, the results of~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{auel2015semiorthogonal} show 
that an $S$-linear semiorthogonal decomposition for a general flat family~${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ 
whose components are twisted derived categories of finite coverings of~$S$ does not exist.
nodes.clean_text: For d le 4, however, the results of show that an S-linear semiorthogonal decomposition for a general flat family~X to S whose components are twisted derived categories of finite coverings of~S does not exist.

conclusions: item[Type 0] Neither of P_i lies on the exceptional divisor in X_i-1 and their images in P^2 do not lie on a common line.
Then widetildeX contains no (-2)-curves and X = widetildeX is smooth.
item[Type 1] Neither of P_i lies on the exceptional divisor in X_i-1 but their images in P^2 lie on a common line.
Then widetildeX contains a unique (-2)-curve (the strict transform Delta_123 of that line) and~X has one~A_1 singularity.

item[Type 2] The point P_2 lies on the exceptional divisor of X_1 to X_0, the point P_3 is away from the exceptional divisors, and the line through P_1 in the direction of P_2 on P^2 does not pass through the image of P_3.
Then widetildeX contains a unique (-2)-curve (the strict transform Delta_12 of the exceptional divisor of X_1 to X_0) and X has one A_1 singularity.

item[Type 3] The point P_2 lies on the exceptional divisor of X_1 to X_0, the point P_3 is away from the exceptional divisors, but the line through P_1 in the direction of P_2 on P^2 passes through the image of P_3.

Then widetildeX contains two disjoint (-2)-curves (the strict transforms Delta_123 and Delta_12 of the line on~P^2 and of the exceptional divisor of X_1 to X_0, respectively) and X has two A_1 singularities.

item[Type 4] The point P_2 lies on the exceptional divisor of X_1 to X_0, the point P_3 lies on the exceptional divisor of X_2 to X_1, and the strict transform L_12 of the line through P_1 in the direction of P_2 does not contain P_3.
Then widetildeX contains a 2-chain of (-2)-curves (the strict transforms Delta_12 and Delta_23 of the exceptional divisors of X_1 to X_0 and X_2 to X_1, respectively) and X has one A_2 singularity.

item[Type 5] The point P_2 lies on the exceptional divisor of X_1 to X_0, the point P_3 lies on the exceptional divisor of X_2 to X_1, and the strict transform of the line through P_1 in the direction of P_2 contains P_3.

Then widetildeX contains a 2-chain of (-2)-curves and one more (-2)-curve disjoint from the chain (the strict transforms Delta_123, Delta_12 and Delta_23 of the line and the exceptional divisors of~X_1 to X_0 and X_2 to X_1 respectively) and X has one A_2 singularity and one A_1 singularity.
nodes.raw_latex:
\item[Type 0] 
Neither of $P_i$ lies on the exceptional divisor in $X_{i-1}$ and their images in ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ do not lie on a common line.
Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains no $(-2)$-curves and $X = {\widetilde{X}}$ is smooth.
\item[Type 1] 
Neither of $P_i$ lies on the exceptional divisor in $X_{i-1}$ but their images in ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ lie on a common line.
Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a unique $(-2)$-curve (the strict transform $\Delta_{123}$ of that line) and~$X$ has one~$A_1$ singularity.
\item[Type 2] 
The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ is away from the exceptional divisors, 
and the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ does not pass through the image of $P_3$.
Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a unique $(-2)$-curve (the strict transform $\Delta_{12}$ of the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$) and $X$ has one $A_1$ singularity.
\item[Type 3] 
The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ is away from the exceptional divisors, 
but the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ passes through the image of $P_3$.
Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains two disjoint $(-2)$-curves 
(the strict transforms $\Delta_{123}$ and $\Delta_{12}$ of the line on~${\mathbb{P}}^2$ and of the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, respectively) 
and $X$ has two $A_1$ singularities.
\item[Type 4] 
The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_2 \to X_1$, 
and the strict transform $L_{12}$ of the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ does not contain $P_3$.
Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a 2-chain of $(-2)$-curves 
(the strict transforms $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ of the exceptional divisors of $X_1 \to X_0$ and $X_2 \to X_1$, respectively) 
and $X$ has one $A_2$ singularity.
\item[Type 5] 
The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_2 \to X_1$, 
and the strict transform of the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ contains $P_3$.
Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a 2-chain of $(-2)$-curves and one more $(-2)$-curve disjoint from the chain (the strict transforms $\Delta_{123}$, $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ of the line 
and the exceptional divisors of~$X_1 \to X_0$ and $X_2 \to X_1$ respectively) and $X$ has one $A_2$ singularity and one $A_1$ singularity.

nodes.statement: Let pi colon widetildeX to X be a proper morphism with fibers of dimension at most~1. Let F be a possibly unbounded complex of quasicoherent sheaves on widetildeX and let H^i(F) be its cohomology sheaf in degree i. The spectral sequence R^ipi_*(H^j(F)) Rightarrow H^i+j(pi_*(F)) degenerates at the second page, and gives for each i an exact sequence 0 to R^1pi_*H^i-1(F) to H^i(pi_*(F)) to R^0pi_*H^i(F) to 0. In particular, if H^i(pi_*(F)) = 0 for i le p for some integer p, then pi_*(H^i(F)) = 0 for i le p - 1 and pi_*F cong pi_*(tau^ge pF), where tau stands for the truncation functor with respect to the canonical filtration.

nodes.statement: Let f colon X to Spec(k) be the structure morphism. If F is a locally free sheaf, then we have Ext^i(F,G) cong H^i(X,F^vee otimes G), and this is a cohomology group of f_*(F^vee otimes G). By Grothendieck duality RHom(f_*(F^vee otimes G),k) cong RHom(F^vee otimes G,f^!(k)). Since X is Gorenstein, f^!(k) cong omega_X[n], hence the right hand side equals RHom(F^vee otimes G, omega_X[n]). Since~F is locally free, this can be rewritten as RHom(G,F otimes omega_X[n]). Computing the cohomology groups in degree -i, we deduce the required duality isomorphism. For arbitrary perfect F the Serre duality follows by using the stupid filtration. Finally, when G is perfect, we replace F by G, G by F otimes omega_X, and i by n - i, and deduce the required isomorphism from the previous case.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $f \colon X \to \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ be the structure morphism.
If ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a locally free sheaf, then we have $\mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^i(X,{\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$, and this is a cohomology group of $f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$.
By Grothendieck duality
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{RHom}(f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}),{\mathsf{k}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}},f^!({\mathsf{k}})).
\end{equation*}
Since $X$ is Gorenstein, $f^!({\mathsf{k}}) \cong \omega_X[n]$, hence the right hand side equals $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}, \omega_X[n])$.
Since~${\mathscr{F}}$ is locally free, this can be rewritten as $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X[n])$.
Computing the cohomology groups in degree $-i$, we deduce the required duality isomorphism.

For arbitrary perfect ${\mathscr{F}}$ the Serre duality follows by using the stupid filtration.

Finally, when ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, we replace ${\mathscr{F}}$ by ${\mathscr{G}}$, ${\mathscr{G}}$ by ${\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X$, and $i$ by $n - i$, and deduce the required isomorphism from the previous case.

\label{proposition:tcai-auslander}
The components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ of~\eqref{eq:dbtx} are equivalent to products of derived categories of Auslander algebras as indicated in the next table:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Type of $X$} & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \\
\hline 
0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\
\hline
1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\
\hline
2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})  \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\
\hline
3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\
\hline
4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})  \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\
\hline
5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\
\hline
\end{array}
\end{equation*}
This equivalence takes the exceptional line bundles in~\eqref{eq:tx-excol} 
to the standard exceptional modules over the corresponding Auslander algebra.

nodes.statement: The component widetildeA_1 is generated by a single exceptional object, hence is equivalent to D(k). So, in view of Proposition~ to prove the proposition it is enough to compute Ext-spaces between the exceptional line bundles forming the components widetildeA_2 and widetildeA_3 of the semiorthogonal decomposition~. First of all, we have Ext^p(O_widetildeX(h-e_i), O_widetildeX(h-e_j)) cong H^p(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(e_i - e_j)). Assuming i ne j and using exact sequences (note that e_icdot e_j = 0 and e_i^2 = -1 by Lemma~) 0 to O_widetildeX(e_i - e_j) to O_widetildeX(e_i) to O_E_j to 0, 0 to O_widetildeX to O_widetildeX(e_i) to O_E_i(-1) to 0, we obtain an exact sequence 0 to H^0(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(e_i - e_j)) to k to k to H^1(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(e_i - e_j)) to 0, where the middle map is given by the restriction to E_j of the equation of E_i. This restriction vanishes if and only if E_j is a component of E_i --- in this case we deduce that Ext^bullet(O_widetildeX(h-e_i), O_widetildeX(h-e_j)) cong k oplus k[-1], and otherwise Ext^bullet(O_widetildeX(h-e_i), O_widetildeX(h-e_j)) = 0. By Proposition~ this gives the required description of widetildeA_2 in types from~0 to 3. In the last two types (4 and 5) it remains to check that multiplication map Ext^p(O_widetildeX(h-e_1),O_widetildeX(h-e_2)) otimes Ext^q(O_widetildeX(h-e_2),O_widetildeX(h-e_3)) to Ext^p+q(O_widetildeX(h-e_1),O_widetildeX(h-e_3)) is an isomorphism when p = 0 or q = 0. For this consider exact sequences 0 to O_widetildeX(h - e_1) xrightarrow\ Delta_12\ O_widetildeX(h - e_2) to O_Delta_12(-1) to 0, 0 to O_widetildeX(h - e_2) xrightarrow\ Delta_23\ O_widetildeX(h - e_3) to O_Delta_23(-1) to 0, where Delta_12 = E_1 - E_2 and Delta_23 = E_2 - E_3. Using Lemma~, we compute Ext^bullet(O_widetildeX(h-e_1),O_Delta_23(-1)) cong H^bullet(Delta_23,O_widetildeX(e_1 - h)vert_Delta_23 otimes O_Delta_23(-1)) = H^bullet(Delta_23,O_Delta_23(-1)) = 0. Applying the functor Ext^bullet(O_widetildeX(h-e_1),-) to~, we deduce that~ is an isomorphism for~q = 0. Similarly, by Serre duality Ext^bullet(O_Delta_12(-1),O_widetildeX(h-e_3)) is dual to Ext^bullet(O_widetildeX(e_1 + e_2 - 2h),O_Delta_12(-1)), and a computation similar to the above shows it is zero. Applying the functor Ext^bullet(-,O_widetildeX(h-e_3)) to~, we deduce that~~ is an isomorphism for p = 0. To describe widetildeA_3 we only need to compute Ext^p(O_widetildeX(h), O_widetildeX(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) cong H^p(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)). Using exact sequences 0 to O_widetildeX(h - e_1) to O_widetildeX(h) &to O_E_1 to 0,\\ 0 to O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2) to O_widetildeX(h - e_1) &to O_E_2 to 0,\\ 0 to O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) to O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2) &to O_E_3 to 0, we conclude that H^bullet(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = 0 if the three centers of the blowups are not contained on a line (i.e., in types~0, 2, and 4), and H^0(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = H^1(widetildeX, O_widetildeX(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = k otherwise. By Proposition~ this describes widetildeA_3.

\label{theorem:dbx}
Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field~${\mathsf{k}}$, and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities.
Then there is a unique semiorthogonal decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dbx}
{\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \rangle,
\end{equation}
such that $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) = {\mathcal{A}}_i$ and $\pi^*({\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X)) \subset {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$, where ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ are the components of~\eqref{eq:dbtx}.
The components~${\mathcal{A}}_i$ are admissible with projection functors of finite cohomological amplitude, 
and are equivalent to products of derived categories of finite-dimensional algebras as indicated 
in the next table:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Type of $X$} & {\mathcal{A}}_1 & {\mathcal{A}}_2 & {\mathcal{A}}_3 \\
\hline 
0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\
\hline
1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\
\hline
2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})  \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\
\hline
3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\
\hline
4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})  \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\
\hline
5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\
\hline
\end{array}
\end{equation*}
The categories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^\mathrm{perf} := {\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X)$ form a semiorthogonal decomposition of the perfect category
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1^\mathrm{perf}, {\mathcal{A}}_2^\mathrm{perf}, {\mathcal{A}}_3^\mathrm{perf} \rangle.
\end{equation*}

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties}
an object ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is in $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ if and only if every its cohomology sheaf~${\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})$ 
is an iterated extension of sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$
where $\Delta$ run over the set ${\boldsymbol\Delta}$ of all $(-2)$-curves on~${\widetilde{X}}$.
Note that ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ by~\eqref{eq:e12} and~\eqref{eq:e23}, while ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ by~\eqref{eq:e123}.

supported on the union of the curves $\Delta$ from ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ respectively).

nodes.statement: By Lemma~ the functor pi^* colon D^-(X) to D^-(widetildeX) is fully faithful, hence the subcategories A_i^- are semiorthogonal. Let us prove~. For this take any object F in widetildeA_i^- and consider the standard triangle pi^*(pi_*F) to F to G. Then, of course, G in Kerpi_*. It follows from the above triangle that Hom(G,G_j) = 0, hence G_j = 0 since it is a direct summand of G. \tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\le a-1}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \to \tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \to \tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})))
\end{equation*}
obtained by applying the projection functor $\tilde\alpha_i$ to the canonical truncation triangle.

By definition $\gamma_j = \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma_j \circ \pi_{m_j}^*$ and its image is contained in $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) = {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$.
Moreover, since $\gamma_j$ preserves boundedness, it actually is in ${\mathcal{A}}_i$.

To see that the images of $\gamma_j$ are orthogonal, it is enough to check orthogonality of the images of functors $\pi^* \circ \gamma_j = \tilde\gamma_j \circ \pi_{m_j}^*$,
which follows immediately from Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}.


Finally, let us show the generation.
Assume ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_i$ and let ${\mathscr{G}} \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ be such that $\pi_*{\mathscr{G}} \cong {\mathscr{F}}$ (it exists by Proposition~\ref{proposition:sod-dbx}). 
Then ${\mathscr{G}}$ has a direct sum decomposition ${\mathscr{G}} \cong \oplus {\mathscr{G}}_j$, 
where ${\mathscr{G}}_j \in \tilde\gamma_j({\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_{m_j}))$ (Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}).
Therefore, ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*({\mathscr{G}}) \cong \oplus \pi_*({\mathscr{G}}_j)$.
Moreover, $\pi_*({\mathscr{G}}_j) \in \pi_*(\tilde\gamma_j({\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_{m_j}))) = \gamma_j({\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m))$,
hence objects ${\mathscr{F}}_j = \pi_*({\mathscr{G}}_j)$ give the required decomposition of ${\mathscr{F}}$.

As we discussed in Section~\ref{subsection:duality}, the functor ${\mathscr{F}} \mapsto {\mathscr{F}}^\vee$ is an equivalence ${\mathbf{D}}(X)^{\mathrm{opp}} \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ (since~$X$ is Gorenstein).

with~${\mathcal{A}}_i^\vee \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)^{\mathrm{opp}}$.
Since $Z_1$, $Z_2$ and $Z_3$ are themselves Gorenstein, we have ${\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)^{\mathrm{opp}} \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)$.

\dots \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ \ \ } {\mathsf{k}} \to 0
\end{equation*}
we see that $({\mathscr{F}},t)$ is flat over $Z$ if and only if the complex
\begin{equation*}
\dots \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } \dots 
\end{equation*}
is exact.
This means that $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}}$ and $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t{\mathscr{F}}$.
The second equality implies that the composition of all maps in~\eqref{eq:t-quotients} is an isomorphism, hence so is each of them.
On the other hand, if all the maps in~\eqref{eq:t-quotients} are isomorphisms then both equalities above easily follow.
This proves the required criterion of flatness.

First, by commutativity of~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma} we have ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z))$.
Furthermore, $\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong P_0$, the principal projective module, see~\eqref{eq:pms}, so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tcez-p0}
{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(P_0).
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} the module $P_0$ is an iterated extension of the standard exceptional modules $E_i$, 
hence $\tilde\gamma_Z(P_0)$ is an iterated extension of $\tilde\gamma_Z(E_i)$, 
and as it is explained in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} these are line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$.
More precisely, if $Z$ is reduced, then 
\begin{equation*}
{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)\quad\text{for some $i$},\quad\text{or}\quad 
{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h),\quad\text{or}\quad
{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3),
\end{equation*}
depending on whether $Z$ is a component of $Z_2$ or of $Z_3$.
Furthermore, if $Z$ has length~2 then we have exact sequences
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tcez-12}
0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0,
\end{equation}
when $Z$ is a component of $Z_2$, or
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tcez-123}
0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \to 0,
\end{equation}
when $Z$ is a component of $Z_3$.
Finally, if $Z$ has length~3 we have two exact sequences
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tcez-12-23}
0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}'_Z \to 0,
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}'_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0.
\end{equation}
In all cases ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ is evidently a vector bundle of rank~$\ell(Z)$, 
and since ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_Z$, it follows that ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is also a vector bundle of the same rank~$\ell(Z)$.
Finally, since $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_Z$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_z$,

Now the last part of Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} implies the last part of the proposition.

nodes.statement: Let Z cong Spec(k[t]/t^m) subset Z_d be a connected component. We apply Lemma~ to construct a sheaf E_Z on~X times Z such that E_Z cong p_X*E_Z. For this, first, note that the filtration on O_Z induced by the natural action of the ring k[t]/t^m has quotients isomorphic to O_z, where z is the closed point of Z, hence the induced filtration on E_Z cong gamma_Z(O_Z) has quotients isomorphic to gamma(O_z) = E_z, i.e., (t^iE_Z)/(t^i+1E_Z) cong E_z. It is clear that the epimorphisms between these quotients induced by t have to be isomorphisms, hence the sheaf E_Z associated with E_Z is flat over~Z by Lemma~. Next, we define E_Z_d as the sum E_Z_d := bigoplus E_Z over connected components Z subset Z_d. Then the first part of the proposition holds. It remains to show that the functors gamma_Z_d are Fourier--Mukai. The functor tildegamma_Z colon D(tildeR_m) to D(widetildeX) by construction (which is explained in Proposition~ and is based on Proposition~) is a Fourier--Mukai functor. By~ the functor gamma_Z colon D(Z) to D(X) is also a Fourier--Mukai functor. Since the scheme Z is affine, the kernel object defining the functor gamma_Z can be identified with the sheaf gamma_Z(O_Z) cong E_Z in D(X) with its natural module structure over k[Z] = k[t]/t^m, which corresponds to the sheaf E_Z by its definition above. The last claim follows from this by dualization (note that Grothendieck duality implies that the equivalence of Lemma~ is compatible with dualization, since the dualizing complex of Z is trivial).

Let $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m) \subset Z_d$ be a connected component.
We apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} to construct a sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ on~$X \times Z$ such that ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong p_{X*}{\mathscr{E}}_Z$.
For this, first, note that the filtration on ${\mathscr{O}}_Z$ induced by the natural action of the ring ${\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$ 
has quotients isomorphic to ${\mathscr{O}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of $Z$,
hence the induced filtration on ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z)$ has quotients isomorphic to $\gamma({\mathscr{O}}_z) = {\mathscr{E}}_z$, i.e., 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fez-quotients}
(t^i{\mathfrak{E}}_Z)/(t^{i+1}{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z.
\end{equation}
It is clear that the epimorphisms between these quotients induced by $t$ have to be isomorphisms,
hence the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ associated with ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is flat over~$Z$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z}.












Next, we define ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d}$ as the sum ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} := \bigoplus {\mathscr{E}}_Z$ over connected components $Z \subset Z_d$.
Then the first part of the proposition holds.
It remains to show that the functors $\gamma_{Z_d}$ are Fourier--Mukai.


The functor $\tilde\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ by construction 
(which is explained in Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} and is based on Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence}) 
is a Fourier--Mukai functor.
By~\eqref{def:gamma} the functor $\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}(Z) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is also a Fourier--Mukai functor.
Since the scheme $Z$ is affine, the kernel object defining the functor $\gamma_Z$ can be identified with the sheaf  $\gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong {\mathfrak{E}}_Z \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ with its natural module structure over ${\mathsf{k}}[Z] = {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$, 
which corresponds to the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ by its definition above.


The last claim follows from this by dualization (note that Grothendieck duality implies that the equivalence of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} is compatible with dualization, since the dualizing complex of $Z$ is trivial).

Let $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$ be a connected component of $Z_d$ with $d \in \{2,3\}$ with closed point~$z$.
Consider the fiber square
\begin{equation*}
\xymatrix{
X \times Z \ar[r]^-{p_Z} \ar[d]_{p_X} & Z \ar[d] \\
X \ar[r] & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})
}
\end{equation*}
The pushforward to $\mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ of $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ equals the pushforward of $p_{X*}({\mathscr{E}}_{Z}) \cong {\mathfrak{E}}_Z$, 
i.e.~$H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z})$ with its natural ${\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$-module structure.
So, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} to check that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is a vector bundle
it is enough to show that the natural epimorphisms between the quotient spaces $(t^iH^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z}))/(t^{i+1}H^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z}))$ are isomorphisms
(the other cohomology groups of ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ vanish by Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big}).
By~\eqref{eq:fez-quotients} all these quotients are isomorphic to $H^0(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z)$, 
hence $d$-dimensional by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, 
hence the epimorphisms $t$ between them are isomorphisms.
This proves that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is locally free of rank~$d$ on $Z$.



For the second statement, let $Z \subset Z_2$ and $Z' \subset Z_3$ be connected components, 
$Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, and~$Z' \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t']/(t')^{m'})$.

Under an analogue of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ 
corresponds to the vector space $H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3})$ with its natural bifiltration.
So, we have to check that the operators $t$ and $t'$ induce isomorphisms between the quotients of this bifiltration.
Since
\begin{equation*}
H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) 
\cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3})
\cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3})
\cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}),
\end{equation*}
and the bifiltration is induced by the defining exact sequences~\eqref{eq:tcez-12}, \eqref{eq:tcez-12-23} and~\eqref{eq:tcez-123} of ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z'}$, 
it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the corresponding line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$.
A direct computation gives 
\begin{alignat*}{3}
& \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h))			&&\cong 	H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i)) 		&&= {\mathsf{k}},\\
& \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) 	&&\cong 	H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_j - e_k)) 	&&= {\mathsf{k}},
\end{alignat*}
therefore, the epimorphisms $t$ and $t'$ between them are isomorphisms, and the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ is locally free of rank 1 on $Z \times Z'$.

$(i)$ 
Let ${\mathscr{H}}^k({\mathscr{F}})$ be the top nonzero cohomology sheaf of ${\mathscr{F}}$; by assumption it is a coherent sheaf on $M$.
Let $s \in S$ be a geometric point in the image of the support of~${\mathscr{H}}^k({\mathscr{F}})$ under the map $p_S \colon M \to S$.
The spectral sequence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spectral}
L_qi_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{H}}^p({\mathscr{F}}) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{p-q}(i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}})
\end{equation}
implies that ${\mathscr{H}}^k(i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong L_0i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{H}}^k({\mathscr{F}}) \ne 0$, hence $k \le p_0$.

$(ii)$ Set ${\mathscr{G}} := p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$.
By base change we have an isomorphism 
\begin{equation*}
H^\bullet(M_s,i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}})) \cong i_s^* ({\mathscr{G}}).
\end{equation*}
By assumption, the left hand side is a vector space of dimension $r$ in degree $0$.
By~$(i)$ we have

${\mathscr{G}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le 0}(S)$.
Moreover the spectral sequence~\eqref{eq:spectral} with $M = S$ and ${\mathscr{F}} = {\mathscr{G}}$
\begin{equation*}
L_q i_s^* {\mathscr{H}}^p({\mathscr{G}}) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{p-q}(i_s^*({\mathscr{G}})) \cong H^{p-q}(M_s, i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}))
\end{equation*}
shows that $L_0i_s^*{\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^0(M,i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}})$ and $L_1i_s^*{\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}}) = 0$.
Therefore, by Serre's criterion the sheaf~${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}})$ is a vector bundle of rank~$r$.
Looking again at the spectral sequence, we see that the canonical map ${\mathscr{G}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}})$ induces an isomorphism $i_s^*{\mathscr{G}} \to i_s^*({\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}}))$ for each $s \in S$, 
hence by part $(i)$ we have an isomorphism ${\mathscr{G}} \cong {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}})$.
Thus $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}}) = {\mathscr{G}}$ is a vector bundle of rank $r$.

$(iii)$ 
By part $(i)$ we have ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le 0}(M)$ and by part~$(ii)$ we know that $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$ is a line bundle.
Denote it by ${\mathscr{L}}$.
Then replacing the object ${\mathscr{F}}$ by~${\mathscr{F}} \otimes p_S^*{\mathscr{L}}^{-1}$, we may assume that $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_S$.
We have by adjunction a map ${\mathscr{O}}_{M} = p_S^*{\mathscr{O}}_S \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}})$ 
that restricts to the fiber $M_s$ over a geometric point~\mbox{$s \in S$} as the natural map ${\mathscr{O}}_{M_s} \to {\mathscr{O}}_m$.
Therefore, it is fiberwise surjective, hence by part $(i)$ applied to its cone it is surjective on $M$.
So, ${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma$ is the structure sheaf of a closed subscheme $\Gamma \subset M$.

By the assumption for each geometric point $s \in S$ we have $i_s^*{\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong {\mathscr{O}}_m$. 

Therefore the map $p_S\vert_\Gamma \colon \Gamma \to S$ is finite and flat of degree~1.
By $(ii)$ we have $p_{S*}{\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong {\mathscr{O}}_S$, so it follows that the map $p_S\vert_\Gamma \colon \Gamma \to S$ is an isomorphism.
Therefore, $\Gamma$ is the image of a section $\varphi \colon S \to M$ of the morphism $p_S$.

The above argument proves ${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{O}}_S$.
Restricting the triangle $\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}})$ to an arbitrary fiber $M_s$ we deduce that $i_{M_s}^*(\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for any $s \in S$, hence $\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}} = 0$ by part $(i)$.
Therefore ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{O}}_S$.

\label{theorem:moduli}
Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$. 
The moduli spaces ${\mathscr{M}}_2(X)$, ${\mathscr{M}}_3(X)$, and ${\mathscr{M}}_4(X)$ are fine moduli spaces. 
Moreover,
\newline$(i)$
${\mathscr{M}}_2(X) \cong {\mathscr{M}}_4(X) \cong Z_2$ and the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ are the corresponding universal families;

${\mathscr{M}}_3(X) \cong Z_3$ and the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ are two universal families for this moduli problem.

nodes.statement: Let S be an arbitrary base scheme and F a coherent sheaf on X times S flat over S and such that for any geometric point s in S the restriction F_s = i_X times s^*(F) is a semistable (i.e., torsion free) sheaf with Hilbert polynomial~h_d(t) for d in \2,3\. By Lemma~ it follows that F_s cong E_z for a unique closed point z in Z_d. Consider the semiorthogonal decomposition D(X times S) = langle A_1S, A_2S, A_3S rangle = langle D(S), D(Z_2 times S), D(Z_3 times S) rangle, obtained by the base change S to Spec(k) () from~ (the second equality follows from and Proposition~). Since by Proposition~ the embedding functors of~ are the Fourier--Mukai functors given by the sheaves E_Z_d, the embedding functors of~ are given by the pullbacks E_Z_d boxtimes O_S of E_Z_d via the maps X times Z_d times S to X times Z_d. For any F in D(X times S), a geometric point s in S, and each d' in \1,2,3\ we have by an isomorphism i_Z_d' times s^*(alpha_d'S(F)) cong alpha_d'(i_X times s^*(F)) in D(Z_d'), where alpha_d' colon D(X) to D(Z_d') and alpha_d'S colon D(X times S) to D(Z_d' times S) are the projection functors of the semiorthogonal decompositions~ and~ respectively. Using this isomorphism for the sheaf~F we started with, and taking into account Lemma~, we conclude that i_Z_d' times s^*(alpha_d'S(F)) cong alpha_d'(F_s) cong alpha_d'(E_z) cong O_z, & if d' = d,\\ 0, & otherwise. By Lemma~(i) it follows that alpha_d'S(F) = 0 when d' ne d, hence F cong Phi_E_Z_d boxtimes O_S(F_d) for some object F_d in D(Z_d times S). Moreover, the object F_d is such that for any geometric point~s in S we have i_Z_d times s^*(F_d) cong O_z for some closed point~z in Z_d. By Lemma~(iii) it follows that F_d cong Gamma_f_d*L, where f_d colon S to Z_d is a morphism, Gamma_f_d colon S to Z_d times S is its graph, and L is a line bundle on S. Therefore F cong Phi_E_Z_d boxtimes O_S(Gamma_f_d*L) cong (id_X times f_d)^*E_Z_d otimes p_S^*L. This precisely means that the moduli functor M_d(X) we are interested in is represented by the scheme~Z_d, and that E_Z_d is a universal sheaf. This proves the statement about~M_2(X) and the first statement about~M_3(X). The same argument applied to the dual semiorthogonal decomposition~ instead of~ proves the statement about~M_4(X) and the second statement about~M_3(X).

nodes.statement: Assume d in \2,3\. Let C subset X times S be a flat S-family of subschemes in X with Hilbert polynomial~h'_d(t). Consider the decomposition of the structure sheaf O_C in D(X times S) with respect to the semiorthogonal decomposition D(X times S) = langle A_3S^vee, A_2S^vee, A_1S^vee rangle, obtained from the decomposition of Proposition~ by the base change S to Spec(k) via. The argument of Theorem~ together with the result of Lemma~(i) shows that there is a morphism f_d colon S to Z_d, a line bundle F_d on S, and an exact sequence 0 to (id_X times f_d)^*(E_Z_d^vee) otimes p_S^*(F_d) to O_X times S to O_C to 0 The left arrow corresponds to a global section of the bundle (id_X times f_d)^*(E_Z_d) otimes p_S^*(F_d^vee), i.e., to a morphism from p_S^*F_d to (id_X times f_d)^*(E_Z_d). We have Hom(p_S^*F_d,(id_X times f_d)^*(E_Z_d)) cong Hom(F_d,p_S*((id_X times f_d)^*(E_Z_d))) cong Hom(F_d,f_d^*p_d*(E_Z_d)), where the first equality follows from adjunction and the second is the base change for the diagram xymatrix@C=5em X times S ar[r]^-id_X times f_d ar[d]_p_S & X times Z_d ar[d]^p_d \\ S ar[r]^-f_d & Z_d The flatness over S of the cokernel O_C of the morphism (id_X times f_d)^*(E_Z_d^vee) otimes p_S^*(F_d) to O_X times S is equivalent to the corresponding morphism F_d to f_d^*p_d*E_Z_d being nonzero for every closed point s in S. Thus the Hilbert scheme functor F_d(X) is isomorphic to the functor that associates to a scheme S a morphism f_d colon S to Z_d and a line subbundle in f_d^*p_d*E_Z_d, hence is represented by the projective bundle P_Z_d(p_d*E_Z_d). Now assume d = 1 and let C subset X times S be a flat family of lines. Decomposing O_C with respect to~ and using the argument of Theorem~ together with the result of Lemma~(ii), we conclude that there are morphisms f_2 colon S to Z_2 and f_3 colon S to Z_3, line bundles F_2 and F_3 on S, and an exact sequence 0 to (id_X times f_2)^*(E_Z_2) otimes p_S^*(F_2) to (id_X times f_3)^*(E_Z_3) otimes p_S^*(F_3) to O_C to 0. Moreover, the pushforward to S of this sequence gives (again by base change) an exact sequence 0 to f_2^*(p_2*E_Z_2) otimes F_2 to f_3^*(p_3*E_Z_3) otimes F_3 to O_S to 0. Since by Lemma~ we know that f_d^*(p_d*E_Z_d) is a vector bundle of rank d on S, the comparison of determinants gives a relation F_3^3 otimes F_2^-2 cong f_2^*(det(p_2*E_Z_2)) otimes f_3^*(det(p_3*E_Z_3)^-1). Denoting by f_23 colon S to Z_2 times Z_3 the map induced by f_2 and f_3, we deduce by adjunction and base change Hom(f_2^*(p_2*E_Z_2) otimes F_2, f_3^*(p_3*E_Z_3) otimes F_3) cong Hom(F_2 otimes F_3^vee,f_23^*p_23*(p_X2^*E_Z_2^vee otimes p_X3^*E_Z_3)) and note that f_23^*p_23*(p_X2^*E_Z_2^vee otimes p_X3^*E_Z_3) is a line bundle (again by Lemma~). The flatness over~S of the cokernel O_C of the morphism of~ is equivalent to the pointwise injectivity of the corresponding morphism F_2 otimes F_3^vee to f_23^*p_23*(p_X2^*E_Z_2^vee otimes p_X3^*E_Z_3), i.e., to this map being an isomorphism. On the other hand, any line bundle on S can be written as the tensor product of line bundles F_2 otimes F_3^vee satisfying~ in a unique way. This shows that the Hilbert scheme functor is isomorphic to the functor that associates to a scheme S a pair of morphisms f_2 colon S to Z_2 and f_3 colon S to Z_3, hence is represented by Z_2 times Z_3.

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable} all sheaves parameterized by the moduli stack ${\mathscr{M}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are strictly stable.
Therefore, by~\cite[Theorem~4.3.7]{huybrechts1997geometry}, the coarse moduli space ${{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ exists and 
there is a quasiuniversal family ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ on the fiber product ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d{({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ which has a module structure over
a sheaf of Azumaya algebras ${\mathscr{B}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ (defined up to a Morita equivalence) 
of order equal to the greatest common divisor of the values of the Hilbert polynomial $h_d(t)$ for $t \in {\mathbb{Z}}$.

This means that ${\mathscr{M}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is a ${\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}$-gerbe over ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$.
Its obstruction class is given by the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ of the Azumaya algebra ${\mathscr{B}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$, 
and a simple computation of the greatest common divisor of the values of the Hilbert polynomial $h_d(t)$ gives~\eqref{eq:brauer-order}.

By Theorem~\ref{theorem:moduli} the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}^\vee_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)} \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}^{-1}$ on ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ provides a family of stable sheaves with Hilbert polynomial $h_4(t)$
and the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}^\vee_{{\mathscr{Z}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)} \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}^{-1}$ on ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ provides a family of stable sheaves with Hilbert polynomial $h_2(t)$.
Therefore, the moduli stacks ${\mathscr{M}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and ${\mathscr{M}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are isomorphic.
Denoting by $\sigma_{2,4}$ the induced isomorphism of the coarse moduli spaces, we conclude that 
the family $\sigma_{2,4}^*({\mathscr{E}}^\vee_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)} \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}^{-1})$ is a quasiuniversal family on ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$.
It follows that the pullback of the opposite Azumaya algebra ${\mathscr{B}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/s)}$ to ${\mathscr{Z}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is Morita-equivalent 
to the Azumaya algebra ${\mathscr{B}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$, hence $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \sigma_{2,4}^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)}^{-1})$.
Since by~\eqref{eq:brauer-order} the order of $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ is~2, 
this can be also written as~$\sigma_{2,4}^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)}^{-1})$.


The second isomorphism $\sigma_{3,3}$ is constructed in the same way, and with its construction we also get an isomorphism of quasiuniversal families and an equality of Brauer classes.

For the first part it is enough to show that 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:isomorphism-functors}
\mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}({\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d},p^!{\mathscr{G}}) \cong {\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}^\vee \otimes p_d^*\omega_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d/S} \otimes p^*({\mathscr{G}}).
\end{equation}
For this we use an argument of Neeman from~\cite[Theorem~5.4]{neeman1996grothendieck}.

First, the functor in the right hand side of~\eqref{eq:isomorphism-functors} 
commutes with arbitrary direct sums since the pullback and the tensor product functors do.
The functor in the left hand side is right adjoint to the functor~$p_*({\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d} \otimes (-))$.
The latter functor preserves perfectness by an argument analogous to that of Lemma~\ref{lemma:phi-d-shriek},
hence the former commutes with direct sums by~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{neeman1996grothendieck}.





Further, if ${\mathscr{G}}$ is a perfect complex, then $p^!({\mathscr{G}}) \cong p^*({\mathscr{G}}) \otimes p_d^*\omega^\bullet_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d/S}$.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:zd-flat} the dualizing complex~$\omega^\bullet_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d/S}$ is a line bundle $\omega_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d/S}$, 
hence $p^!({\mathscr{G}})$ is a perfect complex, and~\eqref{eq:isomorphism-functors} in this case follows.

Now the Neeman's trick comes.

There is a natural transformation from the functor in the right hand side of~\eqref{eq:isomorphism-functors} 
to the functor in the left hand side.
The subcategory of objects on which this transformation is an isomorphism is 
a triangulated subcategory of the unbounded derived category of ${\mathscr{X}}$ 
which contains all perfect complexes and is closed under arbitrary direct sums, hence is the whole category.
This proves~\eqref{eq:isomorphism-functors} for all ${\mathscr{G}}$.


The fact that ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}^\vee$ is a sheaf flat over ${\mathscr{Z}}_d$ follows from the isomorphisms
in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:md-zd} since $\omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}$ is a line bundle.
Using Lemma~\ref{lemma:md-zd-base-change} we deduce the required base change isomorphism.

\label{corollary:birational-isomorphism-zd}
Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ and ${\mathscr{X}}' \to S$ be two du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total spaces ${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$.
Assume there is a dense open subset $S_0 \subset S$ such that for some $d \in \{2,3\}$ there is 
an $S_0$-isomorphism $\varphi_0 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0)$, where ${\mathscr{X}}_0 = {\mathscr{X}} \times_S S_0$ and~${\mathscr{X}}'_0 = {\mathscr{X}}' \times_S S_0$.
Then~$\varphi_0$ extends to an isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$ over $S$.
Moreover, if we have an equality of Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0)} = \varphi_0^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0)}$ then it extends to $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.

Then~varphi_0 extends to an isomorphism varphi colon Z_d(X/S) xrightarrow\ sim\ Z_d(X'/S) over S. Moreover, if we have an equality of Brauer classes beta_Z_d(X_0/S_0) = varphi_0^*beta_Z_d(X'_0/S_0) then it extends to beta_Z_d(X/S) = varphi^*beta_Z_d(X'/S).

\label{proposition:fd-md}
For each $1 \le d \le 3$ the scheme $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is flat over $S$, and
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$F_1({\mathscr{X}}/S) \cong {\mathscr{Z}}_2 \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_3$,
\item 
$F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and 
\item 
$F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^2$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$.
\end{itemize}
Moreover, $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are Severi--Brauer varieties over~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$
associated with the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$, respectively.

nodes.statement: Note that the assumption implies that S, Z_2, and Z_3 are all regular (Proposition~). Furthermore, by base change to an open subscheme in S we may assume that X to S is smooth (hence Z_d to S are smooth as well by Remark~). If beta_Z_2 vanishes then the map F_2(X) to Z_2 has a rational section. Moreover, one can assume that such a rational section is not contained in the rational 2-multisection of F_2(X) to Z_2 that parameterizes singular conics on fibers of X. This means that there is a birational morphism Z'_2 to Z_2 and a subscheme~C subset X times_S Z'_2 which is a family of conics on fibers of X with the general fiber over~Z'_2 a union of three smooth conics from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface. Note that smooth conics from different linear systems intersect at a point, hence the projection C to X fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of X which is a rational 3-multisection of X to S. Similarly, if beta_Z_3 vanishes then the map F_3(X) to Z_3 has a nice rational section, hence there is a birational morphism Z'_3 to Z_3 and a subscheme~C subset X times_S Z'_3 which is a family of rational cubics on fibers of X with the general fiber over~Z'_3 a union of two smooth cubics from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface. Smooth cubics from different linear systems intersect at two points, hence the projection C to X fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of X which is a rational 2-multisection of X to S. Conversely, assume a 2-multisection of X to S exists, i.e., there is a proper subscheme T subset X such that the map T to S is generically finite of degree~2. In the Hilbert scheme F_3(X/S) consider the subscheme F_3^T(X/S) that parameterizes cubic curves containing the fibers of~T over~S. Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of cubic curves there is either a unique curve containing a given pair of points (if the points do not lie on a line), or a pencil of such cubic curves (otherwise), we conclude that F_3^T(X/S) subset F_3(X/S) is either a rational section of F_3(X/S) to Z_3 or is generically a sub-P^1-bundle. In both cases it follows that the Brauer class beta_Z_3 vanishes generically over~Z_3, and since~Z_3 is regular, beta_Z_3 = 0. Similarly, if a 3-multisection T of X to S exists, we consider the subscheme F_4^T(X/S) subset F_4(X/S) that parameterizes quartic curves containing the fibers of~T over~S. Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of quartic curves there is either a unique curve containing a given triple of points (if the points do not lie on a conic), or a pencil of such curves (if the points lie on a conic, but not on a line), or a 2-dimensional linear system (otherwise), we conclude that F_4^T(X/S) subset F_4(X/S) is either a rational section of F_4(X/S) to Z_4 = Z_2 (in the first case), or is generically a sub-P^2-bundle (in the third case), while in the second case the subscheme~F_2^T(X/S) subset F_2(X/S) provides a rational section of F_2(X/S) to Z_2. In all cases it follows that the Brauer class beta_Z_2 vanishes generically over~Z_2, and since~Z_2 is regular, beta_Z_2 = 0.

Note that the assumption implies that $S$, ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ are all regular (Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}).
Furthermore, by base change to an open subscheme in $S$ we may assume that ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ is smooth
(hence ${\mathscr{Z}}_d \to S$ are smooth as well by Remark~\ref{remark:smoothness}).

If $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes then the map $F_2({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ has a rational section.
Moreover, one can assume that such a rational section is not contained in the rational $2$-multisection of $F_2({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$
that parameterizes singular conics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$.
This means that there is a birational morphism ${\mathscr{Z}}'_2 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and a subscheme~${\mathscr{C}} \subset {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ 
which is a family of conics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ with the general fiber over~${\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ a union of three smooth conics
from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface.
Note that smooth conics from different linear systems intersect at a point, 
hence the projection ${\mathscr{C}} \to {\mathscr{X}}$ fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of ${\mathscr{X}}$ 
which is a rational 3-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$.

Similarly, if $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes then the map $F_3({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ has a nice rational section,
hence there is a birational morphism ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ and a subscheme~${\mathscr{C}} \subset {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}'_3$ 
which is a family of rational cubics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ with the general fiber over~${\mathscr{Z}}'_3$ a union of two smooth cubics
from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface.
Smooth cubics from different linear systems intersect at two points, 
hence the projection ${\mathscr{C}} \to {\mathscr{X}}$ fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of ${\mathscr{X}}$ 
which is a rational 2-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$.

Conversely, assume a 2-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ exists, i.e., there is a proper subscheme $T \subset {\mathscr{X}}$ 
such that the map $T \to S$ is generically finite of degree~2. In the Hilbert scheme $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ consider 
the subscheme $F_3^T({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ that parameterizes cubic curves containing the fibers of~$T$ over~$S$.
Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of cubic curves there is either a unique curve 
containing a given pair of points (if the points do not lie on a line), or a pencil of such cubic curves (otherwise),
we conclude that $F_3^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is 
either a rational section of $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ or is generically a sub-${\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle. 
In both cases it follows that the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes generically over~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$, 
and since~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ is regular, $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3} = 0$.

Similarly, if a 3-multisection $T$ of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ exists, we consider the subscheme $F_4^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$
that parameterizes quartic curves containing the fibers of~$T$ over~$S$.
Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of quartic curves there is either a unique curve 
containing a given triple of points (if the points do not lie on a conic), 
or a pencil of such curves (if the points lie on a conic, but not on a line),
or a 2-dimensional linear system (otherwise),
we conclude that $F_4^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is 
either a rational section of $F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_4 = {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ (in the first case),
or is generically a sub-${\mathbb{P}}^2$-bundle (in the third case), 
while in the second case the subscheme~$F_2^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ provides a rational section of $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$.
In all cases it follows that the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes generically over~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, 
and since~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ is regular, $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} = 0$.

nodes.statement: First, let us show that the condition is necessary. If P(K) intersects P(W_1^vee) times P(W_2^vee) then K contains a bilinear form b in W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee of rank 1, i.e., b = varphi_1 otimes varphi_2, where varphi_i in W_i^vee. The zero locus of~b on P(W_1) times P(W_2) is equal to (P(varphi_1^perp) times P(W_2)) cup (P(W_1) times P(varphi_2^perp)). Consequently, X_K is its hyperplane section, hence is a union of two cubic scrolls, hence is not an integral surface. Next, assume that P(K) is contained in D_W_1,W_2. Then there are three possibilities: either item K subset w_1^perp otimes W_2^vee for some w_1 in W_1, or item K subset W_1^vee otimes w_2^perp for some w_2 in W_2, or item K subset Ker(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee to U_1^vee otimes U_2^vee) for some 2-dimensional subspaces U_1 subset W_1 and U_2 subset W_2. In the first case we have \w_1\ times P(W_2) subset X_K, in the second case P(W_1) times \w_2\ subset X_K, and in the third case P(U_1) times P(U_2) subset X_K, so in all these cases the surface X_K is not integral. Now, let us show that the conditions are sufficient. So, assume K subset W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee is such that the line~P(K) is not contained in D_W_1,W_2 and does not intersect P(W_1^vee) times P(W_2^vee). Let b_0 in K be a bilinear form of rank 3 (it exists since P(K) is not contained in D_W_1,W_2). Then b_0 identifies W_2 with W_1^vee and under this identification b_0 corresponds to the identity in P(W_1^vee otimes W_1) cong P(End(W_1)), so its zero locus is isomorphic to the flag variety Fl(1,2;W_1) subset P(W_1) times P(W_1^vee). The subspace K is then determined by an operator b in End(W_1) defined up to a scalar multiple of the identity, and the condition that P(K) does not intersect P(W_1^vee) otimes P(W_2^vee) can be rephrased by saying that the pencil \b + tid\ does not contain operators of rank~1. From the Jordan Theorem it is clear that there are only three types of such b: item[(0)] b is diagonal with three distinct eigenvalues; item[(1)] b has two Jordan blocks of sizes 2 and 1 with distinct eigenvalues; item[(2)] b has one Jordan block of size 3. It is easy to see that in case (0) the surface X_b is smooth (hence of type 0), in case (1) it has one A_1 singularity (and is of type 2), and in case (3) it has one A_2 singularity (and is of type 4). It remains to note that case (0) happens precisely when the line P(K) is transversal to D_W_1,W_2.

First, let us show that the condition is necessary.
If ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ intersects ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ then $K$ contains a bilinear form $b \in W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$ of rank 1, i.e., $b = \varphi_1 \otimes \varphi_2$, where $\varphi_i \in W_i^\vee$.
The zero locus of~$b$ on ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$ is equal to $({\mathbb{P}}(\varphi_1^\perp) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \cup ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(\varphi_2^\perp))$. 
Consequently, $X_K$ is its hyperplane section, hence is a union of two cubic scrolls, hence is not an integral surface.

Next, assume that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$. 
Then there are three possibilities: either
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$K \subset w_1^\perp \otimes W_2^\vee$ for some $w_1 \in W_1$, or
\item 
$K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes w_2^\perp$ for some $w_2 \in W_2$, or
\item 
$K \subset \mathrm{Ker}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee \to U_1^\vee \otimes U_2^\vee)$ for some 2-dimensional subspaces $U_1 \subset W_1$ and $U_2  \subset W_2$.
\end{itemize}
In the first case we have $\{w_1\} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \subset X_K$, in the second case ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times \{w_2\} \subset X_K$, and in the third case ${\mathbb{P}}(U_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(U_2) \subset X_K$,
so in all these cases the surface $X_K$ is not integral.

Now, let us show that the conditions are sufficient.
So, assume $K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$ is such that the line~${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ and does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$.
Let $b_0 \in K$ be a bilinear form of rank 3 (it exists since ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$).
Then $b_0$ identifies $W_2$ with $W_1^\vee$ and under this identification $b_0$ corresponds to the identity in ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_1) \cong {\mathbb{P}}(\mathrm{End}(W_1))$, 
so its zero locus is isomorphic to the flag variety $\mathrm{Fl}(1,2;W_1) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee)$. 
The subspace $K$ is then determined by an operator $b \in \mathrm{End}(W_1)$ defined up to a scalar multiple of the identity, and the condition that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \otimes {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$
can be rephrased by saying that the pencil $\{b + t\mathrm{id}\}$ does not contain operators of rank~1.
From the Jordan Theorem it is clear that there are only three types of such $b$:
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(0)$]
$b$ is diagonal with three distinct eigenvalues;
\item[$(1)$]
$b$ has two Jordan blocks of sizes 2 and 1 with distinct eigenvalues; 
\item[$(2)$]
$b$ has one Jordan block of size 3.
\end{itemize}
It is easy to see that in case (0) the surface $X_b$ is smooth (hence of type 0), 
in case (1) it has one $A_1$ singularity (and is of type 2), and in case (3) it has one $A_2$ singularity (and is of type 4).

It remains to note that case (0) happens precisely when the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is transversal to ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$.

We claim that this decomposition agrees with the general decomposition~ of a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. Indeed, the last two components of~ can be considered as the derived category of~S sqcup S (the trivial double covering of S) embedded via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel E_3 := O_X(1,0) sqcup O_X(0,1) in D(X sqcup X) = D(X times_S (S sqcup S)), and the second component is the derived category of P_S(K) times_P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) Y_2 = P_S(K) times_P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) D_W_1,W_2 (recall that Y_2 maps birationally onto D_W_1,W_2 and P_S(K) by definition of S does not touch the indeterminacy locus P(W_1^vee) times P(W_2^vee) of that birational isomorphism), which is a flat degree~3 covering of~S (since D_W_1,W_2 is a hypersurface of degree~3), and it is embedded into~D(X) via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel~E_2. For the second family flatness is clear and Hilbert polynomial computation is straightforward, so we skip it. For the first family we note that the map~ is flat. This map factors as P_S(K^perp) times_S P_S(K) hookrightarrow P_Gr(2,W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee)(K^perp) times_Gr(2,W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) P_Gr(2,W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee)(K) = Fl(1,2,8;W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) to Q. Recall the embedding of the Weil divisor Y_2 times P(W_2) hookrightarrow X_2 times_P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) Y_2 defined by~. Its preimage under the map~ is a Weil divisor in X times_S (P_S(K) times_P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) Y_2) such that for any geometric point~(K,b,w_1) of Z'_2 := P_S(K) times_P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) Y_2 its fiber is the Weil divisor L := X_K times_P(W_1) \w_1\ subset X_K, i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface X_K contracted by the projection X_K to P(W_1) to the point~\w_1\ in P(W_1). Moreover, comparing semiorthogonal decompositions given by~ and~, we conclude that mu_d* circ T_d is essentially surjective, i.e., an equivalence of categories. \label{lemma:reconstructing-family}
Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces.
If ${\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) = S \sqcup S$ and the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ is trivial, 
then Zariski locally over $S$ the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ can be represented as a family of codimension $2$ linear sections of\/ ${\mathbb{P}}^2 \times {\mathbb{P}}^2$.
In particular, if ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular then $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ is trivial.

The proof is parallel to that of Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2}.

Using homological projective duality for ${\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)$, see Theorem~\ref{theorem:hpd-p1p1p1}, 
we obtain from~\cite[Theorem~6.27]{kuznetsov2007hpd} a semiorthogonal decomposition
\begin{multline*}
{\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_3}({\mathbf{D}}(S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)), \\
{\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,1,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(2,1,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,2,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,1,2) \rangle,
\end{multline*}
where ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \to {\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}$ is the resolution of singularities defined in~\eqref{eq:def-yy3} and
where ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ is the derived pullback of the sheaf ${\mathbb{E}}_3$ defined by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xxx3} with respect to the natural map 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:map-cx3}
{\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3) \to {\mathscr{X}}_3 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3
\end{equation} 
(we will discuss this map below).
Mutating the last four components to the far left 
(again, note that~\mbox{$K_{\mathscr{X}} = {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(-1,-1,-1)$} in the relative Picard group~$\mathrm{Pic}({\mathscr{X}}/S)$), we get
\begin{multline}
{\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}, {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,0,1), \\
\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_3}({\mathbf{D}}(S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)) \rangle.
\end{multline}
We claim that this decomposition agrees with the general decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} for a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces.
Indeed, its second, third and fourth components can be considered as the derived category of $S \sqcup S \sqcup S$ (the trivial triple covering of $S$) embedded via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel
\begin{equation*}
{\mathscr{E}}_2 := {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,0,1) \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \sqcup S \sqcup S)),
\end{equation*}
while the last component is the derived category 
of~$S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3 = 
S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$
(recall that ${\mathbb{Y}}_3$ maps birationally onto ${{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ and $S$ by definition 
does not touch the image $\overline{\mathrm{O}}_4$ (see Remark~\ref{remark:fibers-resolution-dvvv}) 
of the indeterminacy locus of that birational isomorphism),
which is a flat degree~2 covering of~$S$ (since ${{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ is flat over the complement of~$\overline{\mathrm{O}}_4$), 
and it is embedded into~${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$ via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel~${\mathscr{E}}_3$.

Let us check that both ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are flat families of torsion-free rank 1 sheaves on the fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ over~$S$ with Hilbert polynomials $h_2(t)$ and $h_3(t)$ respectively, parameterized by 
\begin{equation*}
{\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := S \sqcup S \sqcup S
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
{\mathscr{Z}}'_3 := S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3.
\end{equation*}
For the first flatness is clear and Hilbert polynomial computation is straightforward, so we skip it.
For the second we note that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is flat.
Indeed, arguing as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2} we can check
that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is obtained by base change from the map 











\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}) \to Q = \mathrm{Fl}(1,7;V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee) 
\end{equation*}
which is an open embedding.

Recall the embedding of the Weil divisor ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3) \hookrightarrow {\mathscr{X}}_3 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ defined by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx}.
The preimage of ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)$ under~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is a Weil divisor in ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)$ 
such that for any closed point $(b,v_1,v_2)$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ its fiber is the Weil divisor 
\begin{equation*}
L := X_b \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)} \{(v_1,v_2)\} \subset X_b,
\end{equation*}
i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface $X_b$ contracted by the projection $X_b \to {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$ 
to the point $(v_1,v_2) \in {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$.
Thus, by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xxx3}, the sheaf we are interested in is the twisted ideal \mbox{${\mathscr{I}}_L \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}(1,1)$}.
In particular, it is torsion-free, and its Hilbert polynomial equals~$h_3(t)$.

The functor $\pi_m^*$ is fully faithful by~\cite[Theorem~5.23]{kuznetsov2015categorical} 
and $\pi_{m*} \circ \pi_m^* \cong \mathrm{id}$ by~\cite[(48)]{kuznetsov2015categorical}.

nodes.statement: By Hilbert scheme argument, the stack DP_6 is an Artin stack of finite type. So, by deformation theory it is enough to check that deformations of a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface X over an algebraically closed field are unobstructed, i.e., that Ext^p(Omega_X,O_X) = 0 for p ge 2. On the other hand, since X has isolated hypersurface singularities, the sheaf Omega_X has a locally free resolution of length~1, hence~Ext^p(Omega_X,O_X) = 0 for p ge 2 and Ext^1(Omega_X,O_X) has zero-dimensional support. By the local-to-global spectral sequence this means that Ext^ge 2(Omega_X,O_X) = H^ge 2(X,T_X). Since X is a surface, we just have to check that H^2(X,T_X) = 0. This holds by.

By Hilbert scheme argument, the stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ is an Artin stack of finite type.
So, by deformation theory it is enough to check that deformations of a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface $X$ over an algebraically closed field are unobstructed, i.e., that $\mathrm{Ext}^p(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0$ for $p \ge 2$.
On the other hand, since $X$ has isolated hypersurface singularities, 
the sheaf $\Omega_X$ has a locally free resolution of length~1, 






hence~$\mathscr{E}\mathit{xt}^p(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0$ for $p \ge 2$ and $\mathscr{E}\mathit{xt}^1(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ has zero-dimensional support.
By the local-to-global spectral sequence this means that 
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{Ext}^{\ge 2}(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X) = H^{\ge 2}(X,T_X).
\end{equation*}
Since $X$ is a surface, we just have to check that $H^2(X,T_X) = 0$.
This holds by~\cite[Proposition~3.1]{hacking2010smoothable}.

nodes.statement: The stack DP_6 is not separated --- one can construct two du Val families X to A^1 and~X' to A^1 that are isomorphic over A^1 setminus \0\, but differ by a small birational transformation over the whole base. The simplest example is to consider the blowup widehatX = Bl_Y(P^2 times A^1) to A^1, where Y = Big(\(1,0,0)\ times A^1Big) sqcup Big(\(0,1,0)\ times A^1Big) sqcup Big\ ((1,1,t),t) mid t in A^1 Big\, and define X to A^1 as the family of relative anticanonical models of widehatX. Then X to A^1 is smooth over~A^1 times \0\ and degenerates to a singular del Pezzo surface (of type 1) at point t = 0. On the other hand, the family X times_A^1 (A^1 setminus \0\) to A^1 setminus \0\ is isomorphic to the trivial family, hence can be extended to a trivial family X' to A^1. Thus, the families~X and X' are isomorphic over A^1 setminus \0\, but have different fibers over 0.

The stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ is not separated ---
one can construct two du Val families ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ and~${\mathscr{X}}' \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ that are isomorphic over ${\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}$, but differ by a small birational transformation over the whole base.
The simplest example is to consider the blowup ${\widehat{{\mathscr{X}}}} = \mathrm{Bl}_{{\mathscr{Y}}}({\mathbb{P}}^2 \times {\mathbb{A}}^1) \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$, 
where ${\mathscr{Y}} = \Big(\{(1,0,0)\} \times {\mathbb{A}}^1\Big) \sqcup \Big(\{(0,1,0)\} \times {\mathbb{A}}^1\Big) \sqcup \Big\{ ((1,1,t),t) \mid t \in {\mathbb{A}}^1 \Big\}$,
and define ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ as the family of relative anticanonical models of ${\widehat{{\mathscr{X}}}}$.
Then ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ is smooth over~${\mathbb{A}}^1 \times \{0\}$ and degenerates to a singular del Pezzo surface (of type 1) at point $t = 0$.
On the other hand, the family ${\mathscr{X}} \times_{{\mathbb{A}}^1} ({\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}) \to {\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}$ is isomorphic to the trivial family, hence can be extended to a trivial family ${\mathscr{X}}' \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$.
Thus, the families~${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$ are isomorphic over ${\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}$, but have different fibers over $0$.

The variety ${{\mathbb{Y}}_2}$ is homologically projectively dual to the variety ${{\mathbb{X}}_2}$ with respect to the Lefschetz decomposition of ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{X}}_2)$ with first block~\eqref{eq:xx3-lefschetz}.

nodes.statement: Let X_2 subset X_2 times P(W^vee) be the universal hyperplane section of X_2. By, there is a semiorthogonal decomposition D(X_2) = langle i_*phi^*(D(Y_2)), D(P(W_1) times P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,1), D(P(W_1) times P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,2) rangle, where the morphisms i and phi are defined by the Cartesian diagram vcenterxymatrix Y_2 times P(W_2) ar[r]^-i ar[d]_phi & X_2 ar[d]^p_X_2 \\ Y_2 ar[r]^-p_Y_2 & P(W_1) times P(W^vee) ar[r]^-p_2 & P(W^vee) and the map p_Y_2 is induced by the embedding W_2^perp hookrightarrow W^vee otimes O_P(W_1). We modify~ by a sequence of mutations to change it to the form we need. First, using the standard exceptional collection D(P(W_1)) = langle O_P(W_1)(-1), O_P(W_1), O_P(W_1)(1) rangle, decomposition can be rewritten as D(X_2) = langle i_*phi^*(D(Y_2)), \\ D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(0,1), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,1), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,1), \\ D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,2), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,2), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(3,2) rangle. Mutating the last component to the far left and taking into account that omega_X_2 cong O_X_2(-2,-2) up to a line bundle pulled back from P(W^vee), we obtain a semiorthogonal decomposition D(X_2) = langle D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,0), i_*phi^*(D(Y_2)), \\ D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(0,1), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,1), \\ D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,1), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,2), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,2) rangle. Next, mutating the second component one step to the left, we get D(X_2) = langle Phi(D(Y_2)), \\ D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,0), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(0,1), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,1), \\ D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,1), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,2), D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(2,2) rangle. where Phi = L_D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,0) circ i_* circ phi^* colon D(Y_2) to D(X_2). This almost proves the result. The only small thing left is to show that the functor Phi is a Fourier--Mukai functor whose kernel is supported on the fiber product Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2. For this we note that by~ the functor i_* circ phi^* is a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel j_*O_Y_2 times P(W_2), where j colon Y_2 times P(W_2) to Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2 is the embedding induced by the commutative square~. Moreover, using notation from the diagram~, the projection functor onto D(P(W^vee)) otimes O_X_2(1,0) is given by F mapsto p_X_2^*(p_2^*p_2*(p_X_2*F otimes O_P(W_1)(-1)) otimes O_P(W_1)(1)), and its composition with i_* circ phi^* is given by F mapsto p_X_2^*(p_2^*p_2*(p_Y_2*F otimes O_P(W_1)(-1)) otimes O_P(W_1)(1)). In other words, this composition is a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel p_Y_2^*(O_P(W_1)(-1)) boxtimes p_X_2^*(O_P(W_1)(1)) on Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2. Therefore, the functor Phi fits into a distinguished triangle Phi_p_Y_2^*(O_P(W_1)(-1)) boxtimes p_X_2^*(O_P(W_1)(1)) to Phi_j_*O_Y_2 times P(W_2) to Phi. It follows from~ that j^*(p_Y_2^*(O_P(W_1)(-1)) boxtimes p_X_2^*(O_P(W_1)(1))) cong O_Y_2 times P(W_2), hence by the above triangle of functors is induced by (a rotation of the twist of) the triangle associated with the standard exact sequence 0 to I_Y_2 times P(W_2), Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2 to O_Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2 to j_*O_Y_2 times P(W_2) to 0. It finally proves, that up to an irrelevant shift, the functor Phi is indeed a Fourier--Mukai functor with the kernel E_2 := I_Y_2 times P(W_2), Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2 otimes (p_Y_2^*(O_P(W_1)(-1)) boxtimes p_X_2^*(O_P(W_1)(1))) in D(Y_2 times_P(W^vee) X_2), and thus completes the proof of the theorem.

nodes.statement: We could, of course, exchange the role of W_1 and W_2 in the construction. Then we would get a slightly different homological projectively dual variety as the result, that is Y_2' = P_P(W_2)(W_1^vee otimes Omega_P(W_2)(1)). Note that the natural maps Y_2 to P(W^vee) and Y_2' to P(W^vee) are birational onto the same discriminant cubic hypersurface D_W_1,W_2 subset P(W^vee) = P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) and provide two small resolutions of singularities of~D_W_1,W_2, related to each other by a flop, identifying their derived categories. So, the homological projectively dual of X_2 as a category is unambiguously defined, but has two different geometric models~Y_2 and~Y_2', breaking down its inner symmetry.

We could, of course, exchange the role of $W_1$ and $W_2$ in the construction.
Then we would get a slightly different homological projectively dual variety as the result, that is
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb{Y}}_2' = {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}(W_1^\vee \otimes \Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}(1)).
\end{equation*}
Note that the natural maps ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \to {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$ and ${\mathbb{Y}}_2' \to {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$ are birational onto the same discriminant cubic hypersurface ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \subset {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee) = {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$
and provide two small resolutions of singularities of~${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$, related to each other by a flop, identifying their derived categories.
So, the homological projectively dual of ${\mathbb{X}}_2$ as a category is unambiguously defined, but has two different geometric models~${\mathbb{Y}}_2$ and~${\mathbb{Y}}_2'$, breaking down its inner symmetry.

Then we would get a slightly different homological projectively dual variety as the result, that is Y_2' = P_P(W_2)(W_1^vee otimes Omega_P(W_2)(1)). Note that the natural maps Y_2 to P(W^vee) and Y_2' to P(W^vee) are birational onto the same discriminant cubic hypersurface D_W_1,W_2 subset P(W^vee) = P(W_1^vee otimes W_2^vee) and provide two small resolutions of singularities of~D_W_1,W_2, related to each other by a flop, identifying their derived categories. So, the homological projectively dual of X_2 as a category is unambiguously defined, but has two different geometric models~Y_2 and~Y_2', breaking down its inner symmetry.
