nodes.statement: Let X_3 subset X_3 times P(V^vee) be the universal hyperplane section of X_3. By, there is a semiorthogonal decomposition D(X_3) = langle i_*phi^*(D(Y_3)), D(P(V_1) times P(V_2) times P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,1) rangle, where the morphisms i and phi are defined by the commutative diagram vcenterxymatrix Y_3 times P(V_3) ar[r]^-i ar[d]_phi & X_3 ar[d]^p_X_3 \\ Y_3 ar[r]^-p_Y_3 & P(V_1) times P(V_2) times P(V^vee) ar[r] & P(V^vee) and the map p_Y_3 is induced by the embedding V_3^perp hookrightarrow V^vee otimes O_P(V_1) times P(V_2). We modify~ by a sequence of mutations to change it to the form we need. First, using the standard exceptional collection D(P(V_1) times P(V_2)) = langle O_P(V_1) times P(V_2), O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(1,0), O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(0,1), O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(1,1) rangle in D(P(V_1) times P(V_2)), we rewrite as D(X_3) = langle i_*phi^*(D(Y_3)), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,1), \\ D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(2,1,1), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,2,1), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(2,2,1) rangle. Mutating the last component to the far left, and taking into account that omega_X_3 cong O_X_3(-1,-1,-1) up to a line bundle pulled back from P(V^vee), we get a semiorthogonal decomposition D(X_3) = langle D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,0), i_*phi^*(D(Y_3)), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,1), \\ D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(2,1,1), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,2,1) rangle. Next, mutating the second component to the left, we get D(X_3) = langle Phi(D(Y_3)), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,0), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,1), \\ D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(2,1,1), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,2,1) rangle. where Phi = L_D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,0) circ i_* circ phi^* colon D(Y_3) to D(X_3). Finally, mutating the second component to the far right and using the pullback of the standard exact sequence 0 to O_P(V_3) to V_3 otimes O_P(V_3)(1) to O_P(V_3)(2) to 0, we obtain D(X_3) = langle Phi(D(Y_3)), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,1), \\ D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(2,1,1), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,2,1), D(P(V^vee)) otimes O_X_3(1,1,2) rangle. As before, this almost proves the result. The only small thing left is to show that the functor Phi is a Fourier--Mukai functor whose kernel is supported on the fiber product Y_3 times_P(V^vee) X_3. The same computations as in the proof of Theorem~ show that the functor~Phi fits into a distinguished triangle Phi_p_Y_3^*(O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(-1,-1)) boxtimes p_X_3^*(O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(1,1)) to Phi_j_*O_Y_3 times P(V_3) to Phi, with notation introduced in~. Again, it follows that this triangle is associated (up to a twist and a rotation) with the standard exact sequence 0 to I_Y_3 times P(V_3), Y_3 times_P(V^vee) X_3 to O_Y_3 times_P(V^vee) X_3 to j_*O_Y_3 times P(V_3) to 0, hence the functor Phi is indeed a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel E_3 := I_Y_3 times P(V_3), Y_3 times_P(V^vee) X_3 otimes (p_Y_3^*(O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(-1,-1)) boxtimes p_X_3^*(O_P(V_1) times P(V_2)(1,1))) and thus completes the proof of the theorem.

\label{remark:fibers-resolution-dvvv}
The natural map ${{\mathbb{Y}}_3} \to {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{V}}^\vee)$ is generically finite of degree 2, 
and its branch divisor is the Cayley quartic $\overline{\mathrm{O}}_6$ (see Section~\ref{subsection:p1p1p1}).
Moreover, the fiber of this morphism is isomorphic to~${\mathbb{P}}^1$ over~${\mathrm{O}}_4$, and to a reducible conic over~${\mathrm{O}}_3$.
In particular, ${{\mathbb{Y}}_3}$ provides a small resolution of singularities 
of the double cover ${\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}$ of~${\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{V}}^\vee)$ branched over~$\overline{\mathrm{O}}_6$.

Then we would get a slightly different homological projectively dual variety as the result, that is for each permutation sigma in S_3 we would get Y_3^sigma = P_P(V_sigma(1)) times P(V_sigma(2)) Big(V_sigma(3)^vee otimes Omega_P(V_sigma(1) otimes V_sigma(2))(1)vert_P(V_sigma(1)) times P(V_sigma(2))Big). Note that for each sigma the natural map Y_3^sigma to P(V^vee) factors through a birational morphism onto the double cover D_V_1,V_2,V_3 of~P(V^vee) branched over overlineO_6. They provide six small resolutions of singularities of~D_V_1,V_2,V_3, related to each other by flops, identifying their derived categories. So, the homological projectively dual of~X_3 as a category is unambiguously defined, but has six different geometric models~Y_3^sigma, sigma in S_3, breaking down its inner symmetry.

We could, of course, exchange the role of $V_i$ in the construction.
Then we would get a slightly different homological projectively dual variety as the result, 
that is for each permutation ${\sigma} \in {\mathfrak{S}}_3$ we would get
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb{Y}}_3^{\sigma} = {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_{{\sigma}(1)}) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_{{\sigma}(2)})} 
\Big(V_{{\sigma}(3)}^\vee \otimes \Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_{{\sigma}(1)} \otimes V_{{\sigma}(2)})}(1)\vert_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_{{\sigma}(1)}) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_{{\sigma}(2)})}\Big).
\end{equation*}
Note that for each ${\sigma}$ the natural map ${\mathbb{Y}}_3^{\sigma} \to {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{V}}^\vee)$ factors 
through a birational morphism onto the double cover ${\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}$ of~${\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{V}}^\vee)$ branched over $\overline{\mathrm{O}}_6$.
They provide six small resolutions of singularities of~${\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}$, 
related to each other by flops, identifying their derived categories.
So, the homological projectively dual of~${\mathbb{X}}_3$ as a category is unambiguously defined, 
but has six different geometric models~${\mathbb{Y}}_3^{\sigma}$, ${\sigma} \in {\mathfrak{S}}_3$, breaking down its inner symmetry.
